items.q: Will you upgrade another maker’s system?
items.a: For [makes and equipment types serviced]: we assess it, then add or replace our modules. Without drawings, we walk the system down and measure dead legs. Polypropylene (PP) joins other piping by [tie-in method to existing piping]. A hot-held loop, or routine 80 °C sanitization at loop pressure, needs a polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) or stainless loop [whether we quote PVDF].

items.q: Will your work void our original maker's warranty?
items.a: It can: some makers void a warranty after third-party work, so check its terms first. Our position goes in the options report: [warranty position on other makers' systems]. Calibrations are traceable via [calibration provider and accreditation held]. You keep every record we write: certificates, installation and operational qualification (IQ and OQ) reports, updated drawings.

items.q: Will an upgrade restart our performance qualification (PQ)?
items.a: Not necessarily. After a change, WHO TRS 1033 (11.3) sizes performance qualification (PQ) by documented risk assessment: phases, length and sampling. EU good manufacturing practice (GMP) Annex 15 puts the change through change control. Health Canada’s GUI-0029 adds that several minor changes can make a major one. Your quality unit decides; we draft the rationale.

items.q: Can we keep producing water during the upgrade?
items.a: Yes, for generation, pretreatment and capacity upgrades. Each new module goes in beside the old one, tied in during a short shutdown. If your tank cannot cover it, plan temporary water: [temporary RO or EDI units, flow L/h]. Occupied hospitals and lab buildings stay supplied the same way. A loop replacement needs a planned shutdown.

items.q: Will the new controls become obsolete too?
items.a: Yes, eventually: makers retire every controller. Ours are makers’ catalogue parts, not our own. Our service page states how long parts stay available, and how we name a successor.
